svg.text: ARCHITECTURE LAB / THE CORNER — three variants in plan
Revision 06 kit, turned through 90 degrees. Paper only: this script writes no map.
Plan view. Corridor A enters from the left, corridor B leaves at the bottom. OUTER corner top-right, INNER elbow bottom-left — matching the sketch.
Hard 90. Square landing, corridor continues at right angles.
Outer corner chamfered at 45. The pocket stops being square.
Outer corner and elbow both chamfered; a short 45 leg between.
Every number is computed by tools/architecture_lab_corner.py from the section module, not measured off the drawing.
The corner does not crowd — it BULGES.
A hard 90 opens to 8.49 m across the diagonal against a 6.00 m corridor — 41% wider at the turn. The
worry was the inside getting tight; the measurement says the opposite. What crowds the turn is not
the wall, it is the RIB standing on the elbow.
The elbow chamfer is the opposite — it is ALL play.
V3 shortens the racing line to 8.51 m and opens the exit view from 6.6 m to 9.4 m, seen from 8 m
back. It moves better and hides far less. A corner meant to work as a sight blocker should NOT have
The outer chamfer is a LOOKS decision, not a PLAY decision.
V2 changes nothing a player can feel: same racing line (8.94 m), same sightline (6.6 m). It shrinks
the bulge from 41% to 24% and stops the pocket reading as a dead square. Judge it by eye, not by
A rib at every bend removes the 22.5° mitre problem.
A 45° plan chamfer meeting an orthogonal wall needs a 22.5° mitre, and 22.5° will not land on the
0.125 m grid. Put a rib at each end of every chamfer instead: the straight wall dies into one rib
face and the chamfer into the next, and the rib stands 0.50 m proud so the joint is never seen.
HOW LONG MUST THE 45° LEG BE? — a rib at each end only works if there is room for them
Raised by the user, and it holds. Too short and the two ribs collide; a little longer and they clear but read as crowded against the 3.50 m bay used
everywhere else. Both thresholds fall straight out of the rib depth and pitch.
chamfer size c → clear run left between the two ribs
← the most chamfer the lane allows, and still a third short
A plain chamfer can never hold a full bay.
A full 3.50 m bay needs c = 2.83 m, but the lane caps c at 2.00 m. The best
legal chamfer is 67% of a normal bay. The prediction was right — so stop
chamfering the corner and make the 45° run a piece of corridor in its own
right: straight, slice, a full bay at 45°, slice, straight.
Cost: the junction grows. The two walls bend 2.485 m apart — and that is
irrational, so a true 45° turn cannot be fully on-grid. Snapping to 2.500 m
costs 1.0 cm of width, which is invisible.
THE REPETITION TEST — how long may a straight run be?
A separate question from the corner, and the answer has to be a NUMBER, because it becomes a rule: beyond this length, something must interrupt. The
built lab run is 24.5 m — six bays — and has never felt long. This lays out 52 m of the same kit with nothing in it.
13 bays at 4 m — identical panels, alternating lit/off, no interruption of any kind
Walk it in both directions and mark the bay where the rhythm stops giving you new information. That bay number × 4 m is the rule.
Run it once with the lighting alternation ON and once with every bay lit — a repeating light pattern may be doing more of the work than the geometry.
WHAT MAY INTERRUPT A RUN, most expensive first:
Ground given at one bay. Cover
